orientation: During use of the model, the researchers observed that signing with the camera slightly tilted could lead to incorrect classifications. Subsequent fine-tuning therefore included mild camera-roll augmentation within ±12°, together with the other landmark augmentations. These transformations exposed the recognizer to small orientation changes while preserving the intended sign labels. The adapted landmark model achieved 95.27% validation accuracy and maintained 94.87–95.32% across the sampled landmark rotations within ±12°.
architecture: The base study compared landmark-recognition configurations before adaptation for connected signing. The flat Transformer achieved 95.50% validation accuracy, the flat Squeezeformer achieved 95.77%, and the part-wise and global Squeezeformer achieved 96.83%. These results supported selecting the part-wise and global checkpoint for subsequent development. The configurations differ in their historical training recipes; the comparison supports this checkpoint choice rather than general architectural superiority.
components: Landmark-only recognition achieved 95.27% validation accuracy, compared with 67.20% for the separate hand-image branch. Combining the two inputs reached 95.40%, an increase of 0.13 percentage points over landmarks alone. The landmark branch represents motion and spatial configuration, while the hand-image branch supplies complementary appearance information.
adaptation: The combined recognizer was fine-tuned on sign segments from phrase recordings, producing 95.22% isolated-sign validation accuracy. Further fine-tuning on candidate sign intervals produced 95.20%. These adaptations prepared recognition for connected-sign inputs while largely maintaining isolated-sign accuracy. A further interval fine-tuning variant started from the same phrase-adapted checkpoint and incorporated partial-sign examples and training to discourage confident recognition of very short fragments. This variant became the current primary recognizer and achieved 95.50% validation accuracy.
methods: The combined recognizer was first adapted using individual sign segments from phrase recordings, then fine-tuned on candidate intervals resembling those encountered during streaming. Isolated-sign examples and reference predictions were retained to preserve vocabulary recognition. A further interval-training variant used partial-sign examples and very short fragments to address incomplete gestures and discourage confident guesses. Both interval variants started from the phrase-adapted model. During inference, the boundary detector supplies temporal evidence, the recognizer scores candidate signs, and the segmental decoder selects and accepts the gloss sequence.
werIntro: Individual-sign accuracy does not fully describe connected signing, which also requires locating sign boundaries and accepting signs in the correct order. Evaluation during system development compared predicted gloss sequences with reference sequences using word error rate (WER), which counts substitutions, deletions and insertions. Table 13 summarizes five development stages on the same phrase recordings.
werNote: Stages 1–2 use the same training-experiment evaluation procedure. Stages 3–5 use runtime processing with the boundary detector, candidate-interval selection and gloss-acceptance rules. The results document system development rather than a controlled attribution of every reduction to recognizer training. These recordings were used for development and model selection, not as an independent final test.
werStages: Before interval adaptation, the phrase-adapted recognizer recorded a development WER of 35.84%. Fine-tuning on candidate sign intervals reduced WER to 29.65% under the same evaluation procedure.

The runtime baseline integrated the trained recognizer with the distilled boundary detector and segmental decoder, recording 17.70% WER after review of training inputs and model refinements. The change in evaluation procedure means that the difference from 29.65% cannot be attributed to fine-tuning alone.

Partial-sign training addressed incomplete gestures encountered during connected signing. With the accompanying runtime settings, this configuration recorded 15.49% WER. Under those same settings, the configuration without partial-sign training recorded 18.58%.

Further development addressed sign ordering and acceptance, reaching 12.83% WER. Transition-example fine-tuning subsequently retained this result while addressing the evaluated transition cases. Intermediate variants did not improve uniformly; the shorter-fragment and rejection variant recorded 15.93% before further runtime refinements.
finalIntro: Following model development and evaluation, ATLAS integrated the selected recognition, boundary-detection and English-generation components into a mobile application. Each component performs a distinct task within the pipeline.
finalParts: Visual extraction. The landmark extractor obtains structured hand, face and upper-body points from device-camera images. MobileCLIP2-S0 encodes cropped hand images to supply complementary appearance features.

Sign recognition. The final recognizer combines an adapted part-wise and global Squeezeformer landmark branch with a temporal Squeezeformer hand-image branch through a learned fusion classifier. The selected recognizer incorporates interval fine-tuning with partial-sign and rejection examples. Its primary output supplies the reported 95.50% isolated-sign validation accuracy, with transition-refined evidence used selectively for evaluated sign transitions.

Boundary detection. A separate four-layer Transformer predicts whether a frame is outside a sign, at its beginning or within it. It was trained through knowledge distillation from the frozen Sign Language Segmentation teacher. The student operates on landmark features and provides temporal evidence for candidate sign intervals; it does not determine the sign's vocabulary label.

Sequence decoding and gloss management. The segmental decoder combines boundary estimates, recognition scores and movement evidence to select and accept signs. Ordering and acceptance rules support the resulting gloss sequence, which is maintained in the visible gloss buffer. These processing rules are distinct from the trained recognition and boundary models.

English generation and speech. A fine-tuned T5-efficient-tiny model converts accepted glosses into English. Incremental generation prepares output as glosses accumulate and retains completed sentences. The Finish control finalizes the remaining text for display and local text-to-speech output.

On-device execution. The recognition, boundary and hand-image components use FP16 exports. T5-efficient-tiny uses FP32 encoder and decoder exports, which are two computational parts of the same language model. The mobile application connects these components with the device camera and user controls.
training: The base landmark classifier was trained for 130 recorded epochs, with the selected checkpoint at epoch 100 achieving 96.83% accuracy in the base validation study. This checkpoint supplied the starting model for subsequent adaptation. The current primary recognizer underwent eight planned epochs of interval fine-tuning with partial-sign and rejection examples. Epoch 4 was selected because it first achieved the lowest development WER while meeting isolated-recognition accuracy requirements; later epochs matched that WER. Checkpoint selection therefore used sequence performance and recognition retention rather than training loss alone.
conversion: The FP16 recognizer export was evaluated using the same prepared landmark and hand-image inputs as the trained model. The primary recognition output retained 95.50% validation accuracy after conversion, although one predicted label changed. Equal aggregate accuracy therefore did not imply identical predictions for every input.
storage: The FP16 recognizer deployment package occupies 26.56 MB. This measures the complete recognizer package in decimal megabytes, rather than working memory or the size of the complete application.
phone: On iPhone 13, the evaluated configuration recorded a median processing time of 31.14 ms per processed frame during two camera-paced replays of a development recording. Timing covered frame preparation, landmark and hand-image processing, and recognition. Camera capture, model loading, interface presentation, English generation and speech output were outside the timed work. This measurement describes frame computation rather than the delay before a gloss is displayed.
